item.title: What the Success of "Backrooms" Tells Us About Ourselves
item.description:
Fear

What the Success of "Backrooms" Tells Us About Ourselves

Why empty yellow rooms with buzzing lights can be scarier than fanged monsters.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • "Backrooms" frightens with empty rooms rather than monsters, and audiences paid close to $400 million for it.
  • Creepiness arises when we sense an agent whose intentions we cannot read.
  • "Backrooms" denies us what we look for in a safe place: a view and somewhere to hide.

The 2026 horror film Backrooms became one of the surprise hits of the year. Made for about $10 million, it has taken in close to $400 million worldwide, making it the biggest box-office success in the history of its distributor, A24. The film follows the troubled owner of a furniture store who discovers a doorway in his basement. It leads to another dimension: an endless maze of eerily distorted office rooms, apparently haunted by strange creatures.

The film's backstory is at least as fascinating as the film itself. The Backrooms began life as a "creepypasta," a bit of digital horror that gets copy-pasted across the internet. In 2019, users on a paranormal-themed board on the forum 4chan were sharing images that just felt "off." One showed an empty room with yellow wallpaper and a stained carpet.

An anonymous user added a caption, and the Backrooms were born:

If you're not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you'll end up in the Backrooms, where it's nothing but the stink of old moist carpet, the madness of mono-yellow, the endless background noise of fluorescent lights at maximum hum-buzz, and approximately six hundred million square miles of randomly segmented empty rooms to be trapped in.
God save you if you hear something wandering around nearby, because it sure as hell has heard you.

"Noclipping" is a video-game cheat that lets the player pass through walls and floors. Fans went on to build the Backrooms into a sprawling mythology of "levels" and "entities," and in 2022, a 16-year-old YouTuber, Kane Parsons, turned it into a series of found-footage shorts. Four years later, he directed the feature film.

Here's the thing, though: The photo shows nothing frightening. Online sleuths have traced it to a hobby store in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, photographed during a renovation in 2002. Everything frightening comes from the caption, and from what it invites us to imagine. That is a clue to how the Backrooms works on us.

The Horror of Almost Nothing

Backrooms belongs to a strand of horror, sometimes called "elevated horror," that favors dread over the startles of jump scares and the gross-outs of broken bodies. My colleague Jens Kjeldgaard-Christiansen (2024) arranges horror's scares along a scale of psychological sophistication. At one end are jump scares, often dismissed as "dumb scares" because they rely on a simple startle reflex. Next are immediate, concrete threats—such as monsters—that produce fear. Further up the scale are threats whose presence we have to infer, which cause anxiety and apprehension, and at the far end are abstract threats that disorient us. Backrooms aims mainly at the upper end of that scale. Through sounds and glimpses, such as distant footsteps or a fleeting shadow, it keeps suggesting that something is out there, roaming those endless, yellow hallways.

Why is that so effective? The psychologists Francis McAndrew and Sara Koehnke (2016) found that creepiness is a response to ambiguous threat: We don't know if there is danger, or what kind of danger it is. But not every ambiguous threat is creepy. A coughing stranger is an ambiguous infection risk, but hardly a creep. Kjeldgaard-Christiansen and I have therefore proposed an amendment: Creepiness arises from disrupted mentalization (Kjeldgaard-Christiansen & Clasen, 2023). We get creeped out when we cannot read the mind of another being, so that it seems threateningly unpredictable.

The Backrooms is full of such cues. Someone built these rooms, placed the furniture, switched on the lights. But who, and why? The caption ends on exactly this note: Something is wandering nearby, and it has heard you.

Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor) in Backrooms (2026). Far down the corridor, a silhouetted figure stands in the light, and we cannot tell what it is or what it wants.
Source: "Backrooms," 2026, photo courtesy of A24

The rooms themselves add to the effect. They are ordinary office décor gone subtly wrong, with odd proportions and endless repetition. The researchers Alexander Diel and Michael Lewis (2022) found that buildings that deviate slightly from what we expect are rated as eerier — an "uncanny valley" of places.

Lost in a Bad Place

The film also taps into a primal fear of being lost in a bad place. According to prospect-refuge theory, proposed by the geographer Jay Appleton (1975), we prefer landscapes that offer both prospect and refuge: an open view and a place to hide. The Backrooms offer neither. There are no landmarks and no exit. Every corner may hide something, and there is always another corner. McAndrew (2020) lists poor visibility and restricted movement among the features that make places creepy.

What It Tells Us About Ourselves

Some critics read the film as a portrait of a generation's fear of spending eternity in a meaningless office landscape. But first and foremost, it targets something much older: a mind tuned to detect hidden agents and dangerous places. Like The Blair Witch Project before it, Backrooms did not succeed despite showing us almost nothing. It succeeded because our minds are so eager to fill the void, and so quick to fill it with danger. We are a fearful species, but also a fear-loving one—and that's why we flock to movies such as Backrooms to be scared.

item.title: Are We Wired to Love Beyond Human Relationships?
item.description:
Environment

Are We Wired to Love Beyond Human Relationships?

Personal Perspective: Can loving "all that is" change the illusion of separateness?

Posted November 24, 2026

Yesterday I came home from time away with my family—raucous, fun days that felt like summer camp, with lots of time spent in nature. As I was enjoying breakfast on my own—the crossword puzzle, toast, and my DD Refresher—my daughter burst onto the scene, full of energy and light, and interrupted my quiet morning with a loud question: “What happened to this poor plant?”

I looked up. A small plant sat wilting in its pot, right in front of my eyes, right beside a pitcher of water. I had completely ignored the plant, and I immediately felt guilty. My daughter picked up the pitcher and gave the poor greenie a drink. Within 30 minutes, it had perked back up.

Source: Lisa Langhammer/used with permission

What unsettled me was not just that I had forgotten to water a plant. It was that I had spent days enjoying nature and still failed to notice a living thing's need at my own breakfast table. My daughter saw what I had missed. Her attention made me question where I draw the edges of relationship.

I consider myself relational. I write and speak about the biological imperative to reach out to one another and connect—an impulse rooted in our DNA and physiology. Yet I see a tension between that need and the “power over” dynamics of many Western institutions: Those at the top define “normal behavior,” promote competition over cooperation, and urge people to “stand on their own two feet.” By power over, I mean a way of organizing relationships in which status gives some people authority to define the worth of others. Within such hierarchies, differences can become rankings, and subordinate groups can be treated as having less innate value than the dominant group. Fear can be used to sustain these arrangements, keeping people under chronic stress. In these systems, the fear generates prolonged sympathetic nervous system activation, which disintegrates the mind, body, and relationships.

I see the same power over logic in the treatment of the natural world. When people are valued mainly for their usefulness to those with power, nature, too, can become an asset to exploit for individual needs. In both cases, relationship gives way to a question of what can be taken.

The plant's responsiveness left me with a question: What would happen if I brought the same passion I have for human connection to my relationships with other living beings? Could “wired for love” become an invitation to notice connection beyond the human world, even when love is not quite the right word?

What would happen if I began to think of plants and trees as having their own “love language”—a metaphor for their ways of connecting, rather than a claim that they love as humans do? My daughter assures me they do, and she has always been more aligned and in tune with nature than I have. Reading about these relationships has been eye-opening. Peter Wohlleben describes underground mycelial networks associated with tree roots as pathways of exchange and communication. In that account, the relationship works in both directions: Trees also provide nutrients to the fungi through their root systems.

EcoTree describes a mutual relationship between the trees and fungi as they exchange resources. Its account gives two ranges: 30 to 40 percent of the minerals captured by the mycelial network are returned to roots, while roots provide fungi with 20 to 40 percent of the carbohydrates produced through photosynthesis. The same account describes pioneer plants—plants that colonize virgin areas—as compensating for the absence of mycorrhizae by developing root structures that mimic mycelial filaments. For me, these details bring reciprocity into view: The relationship described is not simply one organism taking from another but rather a mutual exchange.

The account also describes relationships that extend beyond nutrient exchange to defense. One example is a tree under insect attack releasing chemicals through its root system; other trees respond by releasing bitter tannins that predators dislike. A separate example concerns airborne compounds: in the 1920s, Russian biologist Tokin coined the term “phytoncides” to describe substances that travel through the air and kill microbes.

What would it look like if, as a society, we embraced relationality with “all that is,” to use Connie Gunderson's phrase? For me, that would mean understanding ourselves not as separate from nature, but as part of it. It would also mean questioning the lines we draw between ourselves and others, including people of different racial and ethnic backgrounds. Connection need not erase difference; instead, it asks us not to mistake difference for separateness or lesser value.

Source: Lisa Langhammer/used with permission

I strongly believe that widening our attention to include other living beings is a place to begin. My hope is that this practice can help us move away from the sympathetic nervous system dominance—and the fear and anger—that I associate with power over systems. It is not, by itself, a remedy for those systems. But my daughter offered a small example of another way to relate: Notice the need in front of you, and respond. That morning, connection began with a pitcher of water.

item.title: Humor in the ICU
item.description:
Humor

Humor in the ICU

The unexpected role of humor in finding resilience amid critical care.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Even in life-threatening situations, patients and colleagues can find moments of unexpected laughter.
  • Humor can help physicians build resilience while navigating the emotional weight of critical care.
  • A shared smile can remind patients, families, and physicians of the humanity at the heart of medicine.

I was likely the oldest fellow in the nation. I had switched from a long, happy career in headache medicine, largely a calm, outpatient practice, to the challenging world of neurocritical care.

Here I was, entering a field I knew nothing about, critical care medicine, at age 60. My attendings, mostly emergency room doctors, were often half my age!

Dr. Tarvez Tucker
Source: Tarvez Tucker

Basically, I was terrified daily. Life Flight would arrive with a crashing subarachnoid patient, and I stood at the foot of the bed wondering what I should do next, what have I missed, how do I dodge the inevitable.

When I was faced with the chaos of treating hemorrhagic shock or sky-high intracranial pressures, my sense of humor evolved. As a headache doctor, my days had been relatively predictable. I listened to migraine stories and occasionally shared a laugh about the frustrations of missing keen life events “just because I had a headache.” But my sense of humor was gentle then, rarely requiring an explanation.

Now, faced with patients and families confronting unimaginable loss from catastrophic brain injuries, somewhere along the way, my sense of humor changed. I suddenly saw a chance remark, or lighthearted musing from a person facing death squarely in the face, as strikingly funny. Because patients are funny, and at times, unbelievably brave.

We had an older man with Tourette’s and a cervical spine fracture, waiting for hemodynamic stabilization before our neurosurgeons would take him to the OR for decompression. We poked him with a pin every hour on the hour, watching carefully for an ascending sensory level that would indicate his respirations were threatened. We placed a Foley and used digital stimulation when he developed an ileus. He tolerated this quietly for two days, but then, as he exited the ICU on a gurney under the watchful eye of the anesthesia team, he blurted out with some glee:

“Tell Doctor Tucker, the mother-f***r, goodbye and good riddance!!” We burst out laughing!

Swearing seems to relieve the tension. One of our older general surgeons, technically without peer, looked at us incredulously when we asked him to obtain consent for a tracheostomy from a locked-in patient who could only blink his eyes to assent. That evening, gray with fatigue from a long abdominal obstruction surgical case, he took one look at our patient, for whom he would need to painstakingly get consent one blink at a time, and said to us…

"How many blinks to f***-off?" But, of course, he stayed late and got consent.

Sometimes a timely, irreverent comment brings a smile in our work room late at night. It’s not that humor indicates a loss of our sensitivity to suffering; it’s that we develop humor to live and work beside suffering.

I often tell a story to our residents and fellows of a young woman who was called to see her younger brother, who had been struck by a car and lay quietly, but his face deeply bruised and swollen. She walked into his ICU room and immediately lost consciousness. She had Takotsubo’s stress cardiomyopathy (the broken heart syndrome), which caused cardiac arrest the moment she saw him. She was quickly resuscitated and recovered completely.

But I ask my team, tongue in cheek, if they have ever had a relative they weren’t fond of…and might like to do away with. I say, “Consider “happy heart syndrome…” Give her a surprise birthday party! Have all the guests hide in the dark at her house, balloons and toy horns ready; she opens the door, the lights suddenly go on, the balloons burst, and she keels over…dead.

No forensic pathologist could ever implicate you in her death. No toxins were given, no stab wounds to the heart, no malicious intent. The perfect crime.

Source: Brett Jordan / Unsplash

Humor is more resilience than indifference. We do have to be careful not to laugh too loud in our workroom, as families nearby hold the hands of their fading, dying loved ones.

But humor reminds us that in the fragile world of critical care medicine, it is our humanity that steels us to come back to work the next night, and the next. If we can smile sometimes, in the face of sadness, we see that smile reflected in the faces of our patients and those who love them.

item.title: The Worst Time to Open ChatGPT Is Right After a Fight
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Worst Time to Open ChatGPT Is Right After a Fight

AI is built to agree with you, and that's the last thing you need after a fight.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • AI does not give one fixed answer, so the same prompt produces different responses for different people.
  • Because AI adjusts toward what it predicts you want, it tends to confirm your view rather than test it.
  • In one study, people who talked through a conflict with AI were less willing to repair the relationship.
  • When a choice carries real weight, a person who is willing to disagree with you is more useful.
Ask a human for relationship support instead of AI.
Source: Ron Lach / Pexels

When I teach about how people use AI for emotional support, I run a live demo using ChatGPT. One prompt I use every time is "I'm having a panic attack on a plane, can you help?" It is a good example of how AI handles very specific requests from people (and usually handles them well). The challenge is that ChatGPT, like all AIs, responds differently every single time. Even with the same exact prompt, I am sometimes caught off guard by how different the response is.

AI is not a fixed thing the way an app is. In Word or Docs, when I tell you to go to File > Print, your version works exactly the same way mine does.

AI is not like that. That variation is harmless when you're asking about a panic attack. It's something else when you're asking who was right in a fight.

Instance Versus Software

Each chat is its own instance. The moment you start typing, you are having a conversation no one else is having, shaped by your exact words, your specific settings and instructions, everything earlier in the chat, whatever the system remembers about you, the version you happen to be on, and a built-in bit of randomness.

On top of all that, it adapts. It is constantly adjusting toward what it predicts you, specifically, want from it. So the response is not simply produced by AI. It is shaped by you. Two people can ask an identical question and get pulled in opposite directions because the system is meeting each of them where it thinks they are.

For ordinary tasks, this tendency won’t change your life. If you want help wording an email, it does not matter that your version differs from mine. It matters more when you bring it something personal.

Support After a Fight

When you turn to AI for relationship advice, that difference can cause harm. A 2026 study published in Science by Cheng et al. looked at what AI does when people bring it a conflict. Participants described a real disagreement with someone in their life and talked it through with AI. Those who interacted with a validating AI came away more convinced they were right and less willing to repair things, after a single conversation.

Let that breathe for a moment.

You have a fight with your partner, your parent, or a close friend. You are upset, so you open the tool that is tuned to agree with you, and it tells you, in effect, that you are right and they are the problem. It feels like support. It feels like an outside opinion confirming what you already sensed.

And now there is distance between you and this person you care for. But it is not an outside opinion. It is your own version of events, reflected back and strengthened by a system built to keep you feeling good enough to keep using it. It’s your own personalized echo chamber.

And if the person you fought with opens up their AI, they are also more likely to be told they are right and that you are the problem.

What happens to your relationship then? What happens when there are two people, each more certain than before they were right, each waiting for the other to apologize?

None of this means AI is useless when you are struggling. It means you have to know what it is handing you. Its agreement is the design doing its job.

So when something matters, whether it is a hard decision, your health, or an important relationship, take it to someone who is not built to please you. The whole value of another person is that they can tell you when you are fooling yourself.

AI will give each of us our own version of the story, the one where we come out OK. That is what makes it so easy to talk to. It is also why, when a relationship is on the line, it may be the last place you should go for the truth.

item.title: Direct Your Gratitude to a Person
item.description:
Gratitude

Direct Your Gratitude to a Person

Gratitude is not just feeling grateful. It often requires a specific target.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Gratitude for things going well in one's life can be described as inward-facing gratitude.
  • Outward-facing gratitude is concerned with delivering thanks to a specific target or recipient.
  • Chronic pain sufferers and others struggling to feel grateful highlight others' kindness as gratitude sources.
Source: Sami Abdullah/Pexels

As someone who is not naturally grateful, I dread hearing these words at Thanksgiving meals:

“Can we go around the table and share what we are thankful for?”

People’s responses to this question generally follow the format, “I am grateful/thankful for __________.” I am grateful for good health. I am thankful for a recent promotion. I am grateful for the breathtaking nature around me. Some people might simply declare, “I am just so thankful,” without citing any reason.

The sentiment captured in these responses is a feeling of gratitude. Maybe you know folks who are bursting with thankfulness and will express feeling grateful at every opportunity. Maybe you are that person.

This kind of gratitude can be described as inward-facing. That is, what is expressed as thankfulness tends to amplify various aspects of the self by naming the things that are going well in one’s life.

Feeling grateful (and trying to increase that emotion) is one way to reap the benefits of gratitude for mental health. But it is not the only way. Outward-facing gratitude, one that is concerned with delivering a message of thanks to a specific target or recipient, should also be a part of how we practice gratitude. In the eagerness to feel gratitude within us, perhaps we have neglected action-oriented gratitude, one that directs thankfulness to a target outside of us. We need to address the imbalance.

As a bilingual person, I find it helpful to reflect on the contrast between Korean and English in the way thankfulness is expressed. In Korea, “thank you” (감사합니다 [gamsahamnida]) is reserved for when there is a clear interpersonal target. More to the point, it is unnatural to say “I feel grateful” in the Korean language; I mean, you could translate it literally, but the average Korean will find the phrasing awkward, as the expression of gratitude in Korean almost always identifies an interpersonal target.

In the individualistic culture that is the U.S., we are prone to elevating feelings, such as the affective component of gratitude. But we need to balance the affective with the behavioral when it comes to how gratitude is understood. We need to look more outside of ourselves to affirm that person who demonstrated unexpected generosity and kindness. And verbal expressions of gratitude to someone need not be dependent on feeling grateful on the inside—if a colleague surprised me with my favorite coffee, hopefully I am moved by their generosity and therefore will say thank you; but even if my heart is not filled with gratitude in that moment for various reasons, I nonetheless have a social responsibility, an interpersonal obligation, to say gamsahamnida to that person.

My research team interviewed individuals with chronic pain and their experiences with gratitude. All of the interviewees said, in effect, that they genuinely struggle with gratitude when the chronic pain and its related adverse consequences become too intense (who can blame them?). At the same time, these individuals clearly described the kind and generous actions of another person as sources of their gratitude. A courageous doctor who tried a new intervention that ended up working. A stranger who came to the rescue in an emergency situation. A supportive partner who heroically took on more responsibilities around the house.

In this holiday season and beyond, by all means, feel grateful. Name all the ways that you are thankful for the blessings in your life. But even while you look toward yourself in search of reasons to feel grateful, also be intentional about looking outward in recognizing the individuals who have shown extra kindness to you, sacrificed for you, or given generously to you.

And with each verbal expression of thanks to another person, with each handwritten or typed thank-you note delivered to another human being, you might find yourself feeling a bit more grateful.

item.title: Life's Solutions: Behavioral Fixes, Reframing, or Insight?
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

Life's Solutions: Behavioral Fixes, Reframing, or Insight?

Influencers, life coaches, psychodynamic and CBT therapists: the choice is yours.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological Issues versus practical problems with solutions? Depends on who chooses the approach.
  • Psychotherapists, Life Coaches and Influencers: which approach to take?
  • How do the various modalities address two life issues: binge eating and sex.
  • A three part series on understanding, conceptualizing and choosing what makes sense.

This three-part series examines the informational divide in how we conceptualize issues some view as psychological concerns but which are seen by others as practical challenges with solutions.

We are inundated with advice. Social Media Influencers have swayed people to change their mindsets based on current trends toward actionable solutions like "You should be treated like a Queen," "Stop talking to your toxic parents," and "Why struggle with yo-yo weight cycles when GLP medications are available?" Life coaches see clients as whole persons with goals, not problems to fix. AI chatbot advisors have added another dimension; why explore your psyche if AI can offer suggestions on how to approach people differently and advise you on how to think?

At the other end of the continuum are psychotherapies that vary in their understanding of the human condition. Here-and-now therapies like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) focus on reframing negative thoughts about why someone remains stuck in life, love, or work and how to cease self-defeating behaviors. Longer-term therapies steeped in classical theories like Freud's and relational theories are seeing renewed interest as people search for greater meaning in understanding themselves, their conscious and unconscious motivations, and their roles and needs in relationships.

There is a difference between understanding psychological intent and motivation and coming up with solutions on how to move forward by shifting narratives in your head, making lists of goals and timelines, and taking a 'no one is going to stand in my way' approach. Psychoanalytic theory examines intent and motivation, narcissistic injury and loss, sex and aggression, and their spectacular influence on how we live. CBT teaches us about the prefrontal cortex and reframing past thoughts and behaviors, focusing on positive change rather than their origin. Influencers promise that willpower and mindset problems can be fixed with the right message or program they promote. Life coaching is not therapy; it is unregulated, and coaches employ many techniques similar to those used in CBT to help clients achieve goals, usually without training, degrees, or personal therapy. These divergent approaches reflect fundamentally different assumptions about human change and whether transformation emerges primarily from deeper self-knowledge and awareness or from deliberate action and behavioral modification strategies moving forward.

Determining why a person chooses one approach over another involves overlap and contradiction, complicated by the impossibility of generalizing mindsets across categories; we are individually unique with distinct historical, familial, experiential, and internal details. Delineating how each approach addresses similar issues is more reliable, and this series examines these mindsets and interventions for addressing two specific psychological issues.

The focus remains on human interventions.

Groundwork

Parts I, II, and III will define terms, share facts, explore perspectives of influencers, life coaches, and two psychotherapies, and examine their approaches to two psychologically impactful issues some consider diagnosable mental health conditions. This series will also ask readers to reflect on their own self-concept and consider what makes sense when seeking help or advising someone on approaches to the issues detailed in two vignettes.

The questions raised are whether all, some, or one available option, like therapy, life coaching, influencers, and AI, might be beneficial for our individual goals, well-being, personal struggles, and relational concerns.

Psychoanalytic thinking teaches us that connection, love, and loss are inherent human needs. We find ourselves in a reductionist, transactional world where quid pro quo never heals a lonely heart and contradicts being cherished for who we are, not what we provide.

The challenges posed by AI are significant. A 'reliable' partner through automation is not better than the real thing, despite what social media asserts. People are imperfect and flawed, not fabrications by AI providing superficial solutions to heal internal unrest, dissatisfaction, and pain. Influencers, life coaches, and short-term therapies suggest human suffering amounts to mere obstacles and shifting narrative is a powerful tool for changing direction.

Vignettes

Tina, a 30-year-old woman who has struggled with weight and yo-yo dieting since adolescence, acknowledges emotionally eating and purging. She wants a relationship but is compelled to stay home eating.

Sam is a 45-year-old man proud of sexual conquests who sees this as masculinity and dominance. He wants a relationship but accepts cheating as inevitable.

Naming Framing

Influencer: Since the term Influencer is social media-created, its definition is shaped by content creators like Wikipedia and Merriam-Webster. An influencer is someone who can alter attitudes, behavior, or decisions through authority, knowledge, or relationship with audiences. Their power comes from self-promotion through media outlets, usually for financial gain and fame.

Life Coach: An unregulated industry that helps individuals identify personal and professional goals, navigate transitions, improve communication, take action, and challenge belief systems. The focus is on the future, using present issues to guide advice, create goals, and confront obstacles. (Whitworth et al.)

Psychodynamic Psychotherapist: A licensed mental health professional who works with patients through talk therapy based on established classical theories like Freudian, Interpersonal, Object Relations, and Ego Psychology. Typically, a psychodynamic therapist is trained in multiple clinical theories and has undergone personal psychoanalysis or intensive psychotherapy. These therapists help people explore unconscious thoughts, feelings, and motivations to explain current behavior and relationships, and examine childhood relationship history that shapes their self, interpersonal, and worldview today. People often become stuck due to unconscious fears about confusing, painful, and vulnerable emotions and thoughts. The psychodynamic therapist uses the relationship with the patient as a primary vehicle through which the unconscious reveals itself.

CBT therapist: CBT is a time-limited, structured, problem-solving approach helping people identify and change dysfunctional thinking and behavior. Treatment is based on empirical, hypothesis-based evidence. CBT is skills-based, time-limited, and goal-oriented..

Statistics

About 14% of US adults received counseling or therapy from mental health professionals.

Data from the International Coaching Federation reports that about 17% of people worldwide have participated in coaching. The most common issues people seek coaching for are health, career, and relationships.

About 40% of US adults get health information from Influencers, with closer to 50% for those under 50. Yet younger adults rate their mental health as fair or poor. (Pew Research Center).

Consider the vignettes above. What approach might be right for you, or how might you advise a friend? Stay tuned for Part II as you consider what the professionals and non-professionals say.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Pain: It's All in the Mind
item.description:
Psychology

Pain: It's All in the Mind

The pain sensation is integrated in the mind.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Pain has psychological complications, but psychological factors can also act as potential pain amplifiers
  • Depression is a common complication in chronic pain.
  • Severity of injury doesn’t always match pain intensity.

The title of this post sounds a little provocative, but it is in fact true. Pain normally starts in peripheral sensory nerves, and the painful signal is then transmitted to the brain through the medulla and the thalamus. But it is the brain (which, ironically, lacks pain sensors for its own tissue), and by extension the mind, that actually "feels" the pain, by processing the painful nervous signal and constructing the conscious experience of the pain, together with its emotional content.

Pain is subjective and variable between individuals. There is normally a correlation between the severity of the bodily injury and the intensity of the perceived pain, but this is not always so. In the case of back pain, which is an exceedingly common modality of human suffering, studies have shown only a weak association between vertebral disc degenerative changes and symptoms: Some people with serious degeneration in their scans are almost asymptomatic, while in some other cases the opposite is the case. This variability helps illustrate the fact that pain is not a wholly predictable process in which a given stimulus always produces the same response, constant and fixed both in quality and in intensity. Instead, individual physiological and psychological factors are involved in the processing and modulation of the pain.

Emotions and Pain

Acute pain has a function, which is to alert us that something is wrong in our body and needs attention. It tells us where the problem is and how serious and urgent it is. Chronic pain, on the other hand, often persists well beyond its initial utility. It is in this regard comparable to anxiety, which also alerts us of possible dangers, but in some cases, like chronic pain, persists after its usefulness has expired. It is a malfunction.

It comes as no surprise that pain should have an important emotional component. It is, after all, meant to be scary and distressing in order to be physiologically useful. When the pain becomes chronic, this arouses a whole range of negative emotions, which may too become chronic. It is also inevitable that the sufferer will attach a meaning to the pain, which may result in a catastrophizing response, or even a damaged self-esteem, as if the sufferer had internalized the painful experience as evidence of a low personal value. In this unfortunate situation, the individual suffers the bodily pain, as well as the psychological hurt that the pain carries with it.

An excessive bodily vigilance and attention to the pain, and a fear of it re-emerging after it has subsided (perhaps only temporarily), have been identified as psychological factors implicated in the amplification of the pain experience. Research has also shown that pain is more intense in those who carry a sense of grievance, interestingly. With all this in mind, it is not surprising that chronic pain is associated with an increased risk of depression.

Psychological Treatments

Given the strong psychological component found in pain, both as a direct result of it and as a catalyzing factor that amplifies the painful experience, it is often worthwhile exploring the possibility of deploying psychological treatments in order to improve the quality of life of the sufferer. Cognitive behavioral therapy, which is widely available, has been found to be clinically effective. Antidepressants, such as SNRIs or the older tricyclic types, can sometimes kill two birds with one stone in certain pain modalities (such as facial pain or fibromyalgia) by targeting the pain neurologically while at the same time providing a useful antidepressant action.

item.title: The Unapologetic Ferocity of Activism
item.description:
Anger

The Unapologetic Ferocity of Activism

A Personal Perspective: What HIV activists taught me about anger, grief, and survival.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • Fear of HIV shaped a generation of gay men.
  • Long-term survivors' anger is often a mix of trauma and a survival strategy, not hostility.
  • On World AIDS Day, an activists' lesson still holds: silence costs lives.

In the summer of 1981, my family was returning from a meal in Chinatown. I was wedged between my two older sisters in the back seat of my mother’s mint-green Cadillac when my eldest sister, Maria, jutted her chin toward the window.

“What a shame,” she said. “They’re all gonna die.”

Along the West Side Highway in the West Village, throngs of gorgeous, sinewy men posed in the late-afternoon light.

It was a startling thing to hear.

On July 3, 1981, the New York Times had published its first story about the disease that would become known as AIDS. Most of the country hadn’t heard of it. President Ronald Reagan wouldn't publicly mention AIDS until September 1985, and by then thousands of Americans had already died.

I was 13 years old, and I didn’t yet have a word for what I was. Certainly, what those men represented was an abomination to my parents. But I understood, in the wordless way that children understand the things that frighten them most, that the virus killing those men might one day kill me too.

For years, Maria’s words haunted me.

Surviving a Plague

A decade later, in September 1991, Larry Kramer stood up at an ACT UP meeting in New York and screamed that we were in the middle of a plague. By the end of that year, the epidemic had claimed more than 133,000 American lives. The 2012 documentary How to Survive a Plague captures the moment, and 35 years on, I can still hear Kramer’s banshee cry.

Then came 1996 and HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy), which combined multiple antiretroviral drugs from different classes into a single regimen. For the first time, an HIV diagnosis was no longer a death sentence. In the years that followed, people living with HIV who maintained an undetectable viral load could expect a near-normal lifespan.

Around the Conference Table

By the time I began working directly with HIV activists in 2015, HIV was considered a chronic, treatable condition. I assumed the dread I had carried since childhood belonged to another era and that young gay men today didn't live with it as I had.

Then I sat around a table with some of the leading HIV activists to discuss a new clinical trial. I came in expecting to collect insights I would turn into a tactical plan. Instead, the discussion turned into a shouting match. "The problem isn't the medicine," one activist said, slamming his hand on the table. "It's how much it costs."

Everyone turned to me, the pharmaceutical representative in the room. Weren't we on the same side?

Why the Fury Made Sense

It took me longer than I’d like to admit to understand what I had walked into. Many of those activists had been fighting for their lives for their entire adult lives. They had buried partners and friends, watched their government turn a blind eye, and learned that politeness got people killed.

On December 1, we observe World AIDS Day to raise awareness, support people living with HIV, and remember those we lost. For me, it’s a day to remember those activists, whom I came to admire as much as I once feared them. Around that conference table, I learned what ACT UP had been shouting since 1987: Silence = Death.

Their ferocity was never the problem. It’s the reason many people are still here.

item.title: Why We Look Away: Examining Our Response to Homelessness
item.description:
Empathy

Why We Look Away: Examining Our Response to Homelessness

Our reactions when we witness homelessness reveal much about ourselves.

Posted November 24, 2026

Key points
  • We can examine the psychology underlying the experience of witnessing homelessness.
  • Homelessness is a circumstance, not an identity.
  • Understanding five common reactions to homelessness may change how people view these individuals.

“We do not see things as they are, we see things as we are." —Anaïs Nin

We see homeless individuals on street corners begging, with signs asking for help outside grocery stores, in bank kiosks trying to keep warm, and pushing carts with their belongings, to name just a few places. We see people in line at soup kitchens or awaiting entrance to shelters. Those of us in the mental health field see more and hear more about homelessness than the usual person.

Homelessness is often discussed in terms of economics, housing shortages, mental illness, and addiction. But there is an alternative dimensional way that we might examine this issue: the psychology behind our response to homelessness. What happens inside us when we encounter another person in need and in distress?

There are five different dimensions of our response to homelessness that I would like to discuss.

First, there is the discomfort of witnessing another person suffering or in need of help. There might be sadness, discomfort, helplessness, perhaps guilt for what we might have, and some revulsion. Witnessing another person’s suffering so openly tells us something about what we all experience at some point in our lives, which is human vulnerability. We depend on a sense of stability, security, and predictability in our lives. We have familiar routines, homes we return to, tasks we need to accomplish, friends who support us. Perhaps viewing another in such dire circumstances disrupts our own sense of permanence and predictability. We may look away, move on more quickly, or stare surreptitiously.

Secondly, we may manage discomfort by creating a sort of psychological boundary between the homeless person and us. We might note that these individuals are different from us. Their circumstances, such as severe illness, lengthy unemployment, and exposure to trauma or domestic violence, are difficult to comprehend. This apparent distance might falsely reinforce the idea that our lives are secure. The greater the difference we create between ourselves and homeless people, the less humanity and humility we experience. On the other hand, erecting this boundary provides us with a sense of distance and difference.

Thirdly, there are social cues that we all respond to. If one sees others passing a homeless person sitting or standing on the street, we may believe that no response is necessary or that others will help. We look to others around us to determine how to behave. For example, if we arrive for a party and note that all people entering are kissing the host or hostess, we may be more likely to behave the same way. Follow the leader is a lesson we might have been taught that perhaps needs to be unlearned.

Fourthly, perhaps one of the greatest barriers to understanding homelessness is our tendency to be judgmental and make assumptions about people who are homeless. We might make the mistake of assuming mental illness, laziness, or unwillingness to get a job, even if it is menial work. We may blame poor judgment or irresponsible decisions. It is a fundamental attribution error, which is the tendency to explain the behavior of another through personal characteristics rather than circumstances that might have befallen a person.

Stigma creates a social barrier. Once we label someone, we stop seeing them as an individual and more as their label. Their history, personality, relationships, hopes, and dreams become inconsequential to the label we assign someone. For instance, I have often heard practitioners call someone schizophrenic rather than a person with schizophrenia.

The reality is that homelessness is a circumstance, not an identity.

Finally, when we are constantly exposed to the homelessness, war, poverty, and violence that are a routine part of our social media today, we may experience what can be best called compassion fatigue. When people feel overwhelmed by the number of problems they are exposed to daily and their inability to do anything about it, they simply turn away. It produces emotional numbing and avoidance. As we travel to and from work each day by walking or driving, or go to the same supermarket and pass the same person on the sidewalk, they, in essence, become part of the landscape of the route.

This same response occurs for caregivers of very ill persons, who might experience an emotional numbing or habituation.

Understanding these five psychological reactions—discomfort, distancing, social conformity, judgment, and compassion fatigue—gives us a way to think about homeless people and their impact on our behaviors.

Awareness is the first step toward choosing a different response. When someone becomes part of the landscape, we stop noticing them altogether. If instead we stop for a moment and examine our own discomfort rather than rushing past, perhaps we can change our responses, if we so choose. Our own unease likely comes from our own sense of vulnerability and lack of predictability in this world.

This small shift in framing can neutralize the fundamental attribution error and restore personal history to the person. Each person sitting on a sidewalk was once a child, has a birthday, had a family of origin, probably went to school somewhere, and had people in their lives who cared for them.

Breaking the spell of social cues requires a conscious choice. Making brief eye contact, offering a warm greeting, or simply nodding in recognition of another person’s presence counters the invisibility of living on the street or having to beg. It reaffirms their dignity. In some way or another, we all want to be noticed.

Addressing compassion fatigue demands a different balance. We cannot carry the weight of every global crisis or every unhoused person on our shoulders. There is a marked distinction between empathy—feeling someone else’s distress as our own—and compassion, which combines care with a desire to help in some way. When we shift from overwhelmed empathy to compassion, we move away from paralysis to practicality.

Returning to Anaïs Nin’s insight, the way we react to homelessness is ultimately a mirror. When we look away, we are often protecting our own illusion of control and permanence. When we choose to look closer—with humility, curiosity, and basic human kindness—we acknowledge another person’s struggle and reclaim their and our humanity. There is an inner person inside all of us.
